reason: A sequence .NET cannot read as a 32-bit integer gives an error from the Sequence element and another from the JSON builder, which then writes nothing. The crates give no error and carry on.
The JSON builder in .NET writes nothing when the sequence in the evidence is not a 32-bit integer.
The sequence after 2147483647 wraps to a negative 32-bit number in .NET, so JavaScript properties are still listed. The crates hold a 64-bit sequence.
The crates hold the sequence as a 64-bit integer and start again at 1 for a sequence that is not a number, where .NET holds a 32-bit integer and leaves a bad value as it was.
The crates' Sequence element writes the session id and sequence into its own data, where .NET writes them back into the evidence.
The crates' Sequence element lists the session id and sequence as properties of its own data. .NET's lists none.
The JSON builder writes the data of the crates' Sequence element, which .NET's Sequence element does not have.
With no address in the evidence the crates' IP Intelligence engine gives an error and no data, where .NET gives data in which no property has a value.
The crates' IP Intelligence engine gives an error when the evidence holds no address it can read. .NET gives none.
The JSON builder writes the IP Intelligence error the crates give when the evidence holds no address it can read.
The crates' IP Intelligence engine writes no data when the evidence holds no address it can read, so the JSON has no ip object.
The crates do not fill the Ip property with the address looked up, as .NET does.
The crates do not fill the IpV6 property with the address looked up, as .NET does.
The crates' model lacks the GeoNameId properties .NET declares.
The crates give Areas as a string, where .NET gives it as a WKT value, which its JSON writes as an object.
The crates give IpRangeStart and IpRangeEnd as strings, where .NET gives IP addresses.
The crates give an IPv6 range in full, 2a00:23c0:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000, where .NET gives the compressed form RFC 5952 recommends, 2a00:23c0::, in the properties and in the JSON.

The crates write a weighted value as value and weight, where the published .NET packages write rawweighting and value. The translation cases write their codes as each side's IP Intelligence data, whichever data file the job uses.

The crates' IP Intelligence engine lists a fixed set of property names whatever the data file holds. The ASN file holds few of them.
Every Device Detection property with no value gives the same sentence, where .NET gives the reason for each.

The crates read the JavaScript type from the data file (data_file_value_type in native/src/dd.rs), but native_value in device-detection-onpremise gives every type other than true or false, a number or a list as a string, so the JavaScript properties are strings where .NET gives its JavaScript type.
The crates give an empty list where .NET gives a list holding one empty string.

With no User-Agent, an empty one, or one longer than the C code reads (a 2,000 character User-Agent, which 51degrees-cxx ignores on both sides), the crates give an empty string or an empty list where .NET gives no value.
For a JavaScript property whose value in the matched profile is empty, the crates give the empty string where .NET gives no value.

A screen size whose data file value does not parse, such as Unknown, has no value in the crates (native_value in device-detection-onpremise), where .NET gives 0. A lost screen size that .NET gives as 0 also passes until the difference is removed.

A number or true or false property whose data file value does not parse, such as Unknown or N/A, has no value in the crates (native_value in device-detection-onpremise), where .NET gives 0 or false. This covers more than a hundred properties, and it also lets through a lost answer that .NET gives as 0 or false, such as a false IsMobile, because a value that does not parse and a lost value look the same to the comparer. Removing the difference removes both.
The JSON holds the empty strings and lists the crates give where .NET gives no value and writes null (properties.device state).

A screen size whose data file value does not parse has no value in the crates, so their JSON writes null where .NET writes 0 (properties.device.screenpixels* state). A lost screen size that .NET gives as 0 also passes until the difference is removed.
The crates' JSON gives the reason a screen size whose data file value does not parse has no value, where .NET gives 0 and so no reason (properties.device.screenpixels* state).

The crates give an empty string or an empty list where .NET gives no value, so only .NET's JSON gives a reason (properties.device state).

The crates give every Device Detection property with no value the reason No value for property and its name, where .NET says why it has none, such as that the evidence it needs was not supplied (properties.device.* noValueMessage).

The crates' Device Detection engine adds the match metrics and the matched User-Agents to its data before the data file's values, so the JSON lists them first. .NET lists them after the data file's properties.
The crates' IP Intelligence engine reads a fixed list of property names in name order, so the JSON lists them in that order. .NET lists them in the data file's order.

The JavaScript holds the JSON, so every JSON difference in the engines' pipeline shows here too. The crates also write the request's parameters in name order with lower case names, because their evidence has no order and lowercases its keys. The values pipeline's cases are not listed, so their JavaScript must be the same.

The .NET 4.5.129 package embeds its template with CRLF line endings, so each line of its script that comes from the template ends with CRLF. The template the specification names and the copy the crates bundle end each line with LF, and the crates write no CRLF.

Each usage record writes the sequence the Sequence element gives. After 2147483647 .NET's wraps to -2147483648 and the crates' 2147483648 is written as 0, because it is not a 32-bit integer. For text .NET's leaves the text, written as 0, where the crates' starts again at 1.

The crates' property values have no type for a point in time, so the agent signature element gives the time as RFC 3339 text, the form .NET's JSON builder writes, where .NET gives a DateTimeOffset. The values are still compared, and are the same.

identifier-layout.md asks a reader to refuse a payload version it does not know, naming the version it found, and the 5 byte header is part of the version 0 layout. So the crates read the version first and refuse a 4 byte payload naming version 2 as that version, where .NET checks the length first and gives PayloadTooShort.

identifier-layout.md gives the creator domain as ASCII text, so the crates refuse a domain holding a byte above 7f with InvalidDomainEncoding, the status the OWID reader gives a domain that is not UTF-8. .NET reads each such byte as a question mark and reads the 51Did.
The crates refuse a creator domain that is not ASCII, so every field but the status is null, where .NET reads the 51Did and gives each field.

identifier-layout.md asks a reader to refuse a text with any character outside the base64 alphabet, white space inside the text included, as RFC 4648 section 3.3 requires when the referring specification says nothing else. The crates refuse these texts with InvalidBase64. .NET skips spaces, tabs and line breaks inside the text in its OWID reader and reads them.
The crates refuse a text with white space inside it, so every field but the status is null, where .NET reads the 51Did and gives each field.

reason: A builder name that matches no builder. .NET looks for builders in every loaded assembly, so it also lists CustomShareUsageBuilder, the builder of the .NET program's own usage sharing element, which is in the program's own assembly, and the three translation builders, whose assembly the program's translation pipeline loads. The crates list the builders added to the registry, which has no translation builders yet.

The crates' usage sharing element says it is concurrent, because it sends from a thread of its own, so a pipeline holding it is concurrent with no parallel group. .NET's ShareUsageElement says it is not.

identifier-layout.md asks a reader to refuse a text holding a character from each base64 alphabet, and to check for that before it reads - as + and _ as /. The crates refuse these texts with InvalidBase64. .NET maps - and _ onto + and / without checking, so it reads each as the clean text.
The crates refuse a text that mixes the two base64 alphabets, so every field but the status is null, where .NET reads the 51Did and gives each field.

A property no engine set reads as null in .NET, because its data gives null for a key it does not hold. The crates' data cannot hold null, so such a property has no value, with the reason No value for property and its name. In translation-no-ip-data the country codes engine sets no property. In translation-bad-item the countries engine fails before it sets any, and in translation-unreadable-after-unresolved it fails after setting the weighted names and before the lists of every country. Each happens on both sides, and the errors and the JSON are the same.
